groups.title: Read an Academic Passage
groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
For most of the twentieth century, textbooks listed four basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, and bitter. Yet as early as 1908, a Japanese chemist named Kikunae Ikeda had argued for a fifth. He noticed that a traditional broth made from kelp had a rich, savory quality that none of the four could explain. He went on to isolate the substance responsible, an amino acid called glutamate, and named the taste umami.

Many scientists outside Japan doubted that umami was truly distinct. They assumed it was merely a blend of the other tastes. The debate was settled only around 2000, when researchers identified receptors on the tongue that respond specifically to glutamate. Like sweetness, which signals energy, umami appears to have a purpose: it tells the body that a food contains protein.

Cooks made use of umami long before it had a name. Glutamate is plentiful in ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, and aged cheese, and methods such as drying and fermenting release even more of it. That is why a little soy sauce or grated Parmesan can make a simple dish taste fuller. Some food scientists also believe that savory ingredients can keep meals satisfying when less salt is used.

groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
Paper money was born from an inconvenience. In the Chinese region of Sichuan about a thousand years ago, everyday coins were made of iron, and a large purchase could require a load of coins too heavy to carry. So merchants left their coins with trusted shops and received paper receipts in return. Because a receipt could be exchanged for coins at any time, people soon began to trade the receipts themselves.

In the 1020s the government of the Song dynasty took over the system and began issuing official notes, generally regarded as the first paper money issued by a state. The idea astonished later visitors. When the Venetian traveler Marco Polo described China in the thirteenth century, he wrote with amazement about sheets of paper that people accepted as readily as silver or gold.

Yet the invention carried a danger. Coins are limited by the supply of metal, but paper can be printed at almost no cost. When rulers needed funds, they issued more and more notes, and each note bought less than before. Repeated episodes of this kind eventually led China to abandon paper notes and rely on silver for several centuries. Paper money, it turned out, depends less on paper than on trust in whoever prints it.

options: How a hurricane forms and keeps going
How hurricanes differ from thunderstorms
Why hurricanes are becoming more frequent

answers: How a hurricane forms and keeps going
questions.explanation: The professor explains the fuel, the rising air that makes the storm 'feed itself', the spin and what finally weakens it.

listening.script: OK, so last time we talked about ordinary thunderstorms. Today, something much bigger: hurricanes. And I want you to think of a hurricane as an engine. Like any engine, it needs fuel. So what's the fuel? It's warm ocean water. The sea surface has to be at least about twenty-seven degrees Celsius. That's why these storms are born in the tropics, in late summer and early fall, when the ocean is at its warmest. Here's what happens. Warm, wet air rises from the sea surface. As it rises, it cools, and the water vapor in it turns into cloud droplets. Now, this is the key step. When vapor turns into liquid, it gives off heat. That heat warms the air around it, so the air rises even faster, and more wet air gets pulled in below to replace it. You see? The storm feeds itself. Now, why does it spin? That comes from the rotation of the Earth, which bends the path of the moving air. Interestingly, that effect is too weak right at the equator, so hurricanes don't form there. And what stops the engine? Well, take away the fuel. Once a hurricane moves over land or over cooler water, its supply of warm, wet air is cut off, and it gradually weakens.

The storm stops rising.
answers: Heat is released.

options: The life of a famous architect in Florence
Why early painters preferred large figures
How windows were shown in early paintings
A method that let painters show depth
answers: A method that let painters show depth
questions.explanation: The talk introduces linear perspective, the 'system' that makes you feel 'you could walk into the room'.

listening.script: Take a look at these two paintings. The one on the left is from the thirteen hundreds. Notice anything odd? The most important figure is huge, even though he's standing at the back, and the buildings look as if they might slide off the wall. Now the one on the right, painted about a century later. Suddenly you feel you could walk into the room. So what changed? Painters didn't simply get better at drawing. They learned a system, and we call it linear perspective. The idea is simple. Lines that are parallel in real life, like the edges of a road, seem to come together as they move away from you. In a painting, they meet at a single spot called the vanishing point. And the farther away an object is, the smaller you paint it. We usually give the credit to an architect, Filippo Brunelleschi, working in Florence in the early fourteen hundreds. He painted a building in his city so accurately that people standing in front of it could compare the two, and they matched. Some years later, another architect, Leon Battista Alberti, wrote the rules down, so any painter could learn them. Alberti said a painting should be like an open window. And for the next four hundred years or so, that's pretty much what European painting tried to be.

options: The largest figure in a painting

answers: The spot where parallel lines meet

listening.script: If you've ever watched an octopus on a reef, you'll know it can vanish in front of your eyes. One moment it's brown, the next it's the exact pattern of the rock behind it. And we're talking well under a second. So how on earth does it manage that? The secret is in the skin, which is packed with thousands of tiny organs called chromatophores. Picture each one as a little elastic bag of pigment, with a ring of muscles around it. When those muscles tighten, they stretch the bag out flat, and you see a spot of color. When they relax, the bag shrinks to a dot you can barely see. Now, here's the crucial part. Each of those muscles is wired straight to the brain. In many other animals that change color, the signal is chemical. It travels in the blood, so it's slow. The octopus uses nerves, and that's why the change is practically instant. But there's a twist, and frankly, it still bothers researchers. As far as we can tell, octopuses are color-blind. Their eyes have just one kind of light-detecting cell. So how do they match colors they can't see? One suggestion is that the skin itself detects light. It's an attractive idea, but I'd call it unproven for now.

options: How shell jewelry was made on Pacific islands
Why shopping has replaced gift giving
How gifts create lasting ties between people
Why the professor dislikes receiving presents
answers: How gifts create lasting ties between people
higher.explanation: Mauss's argument is that a gift creates duties, and the resulting debt 'is precisely what holds people together'.
higher.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?

listening.script: Let me start with a confession. Last week a neighbor brought me a jar of homemade jam, and my first thought wasn't 'how nice.' It was, 'Now I owe her something.' Well, according to the French scholar Marcel Mauss, that reaction is the whole point. In a famous essay from the nineteen twenties, Mauss argued that there's no such thing as a free gift. A gift carries three duties: to give, to accept, and, sooner or later, to give something back. Some of his best-known evidence came from the Trobriand Islands, near New Guinea. There, men sailed long distances to exchange shell necklaces and armbands with partners on other islands. Now, these objects were of no practical use. Nobody kept one for long, either. You held it for a while, then passed it on. So what was the point? The point was the partnership itself. Each exchange renewed a bond between two people, sometimes for life, and ordinary trade in food and tools followed along behind it. Compare that with buying something in a shop. You pay, you leave, and you and the cashier are even. A gift does the opposite. It leaves a debt hanging, and that debt is precisely what holds people together. So the next time you get a present you didn't ask for, well, you'll know what you've signed up for.

options: To illustrate the feeling of debt a gift creates
To show that homemade gifts are the most appreciated
To explain how the professor met a neighbor
To compare food with shell necklaces
answers: To illustrate the feeling of debt a gift creates

Dear Ms. Rao,

I am writing about the mock interview that I booked with you for this Thursday at 2:00 p.m. Unfortunately, my statistics professor announced yesterday that our midterm exam has been moved to exactly that time, so I will not be able to come. I am sorry for the short notice.

groups.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on education technology. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Halvorsen
professor.post: This week we are examining how digital devices affect learning in the classroom. Some universities, and many individual instructors, now ask students to put away laptops and phones during lectures. They argue that screens distract both the user and the people sitting nearby. Others reply that devices are essential tools for taking notes and looking things up. I would like to know where you stand. Should laptops and phones be banned in lecture halls? Why or why not?

students.name: Yuki
students.post: I support a ban. Whenever the person in front of me opens a shopping site or a game, I end up watching that screen instead of the professor, even though I don't want to. A lecture lasts only an hour or so. Everyone can manage that long with a pen and paper, and we would all pay more attention.

students.name: Emeka
students.post: I disagree with a ban. I type much faster than I write, and I keep my notes in folders that I can search before exams. Some students also depend on a device to enlarge the slides or to record the lecture. We are adults, and we should be trusted to decide how we learn best.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

I do not think laptops and phones should be banned completely, but I would treat the two devices differently. Yuki is right that a screen showing a game pulls everyone's eyes toward it, and that problem is real. However, as Emeka says, many students take better notes on a laptop, and some need one to follow the slides. A total ban would punish them for other people's habits. My suggestion is a simple seating rule: students who use laptops sit in the back rows or along the sides, where their screens are not in front of anyone, and phones stay in bags unless the professor asks the class to use them, for example for a quick poll. In my experience, the phone is the bigger danger because of its constant notifications, while a laptop is mostly a tool. A rule like this protects students who are easily distracted without taking a useful tool away from the others.

groups.title: Take an Interview
groups.instructions: You have agreed to take part in a research study about music listening habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

toefl.scenario: You have agreed to take part in a research study about music listening habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 1 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: The last time I listened to music was this morning on the bus to campus. The ride takes about twenty-five minutes, and I almost always put my headphones on as soon as I sit down. Today I listened to a playlist of quiet piano music, because I had a presentation in my first class and I wanted to feel calm. Usually I prefer pop songs with a strong beat, but when I am nervous, music without words helps me organize my thoughts. By the time I got off the bus, I felt much more relaxed and ready to speak.

listening.script: Thank you for joining me today. To start, please tell me about the last time you listened to music. Where were you, what were you listening to, and why did you choose it?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: It depends on the task, but most of the time I need silence. When I read a difficult chapter or write an essay, songs with lyrics pull my attention away, because I start following the words instead of my own ideas. I have tried it many times, and I always work more slowly. However, for simple tasks, such as copying my notes or cleaning up my files, I enjoy having music on. It makes boring work feel shorter. So my rule is easy: silence for thinking and music for routine jobs.

listening.script: Some people like to have music playing while they study or work. Others need silence to concentrate. Which is true for you, and why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I partly disagree. It is true that someone wearing headphones is less likely to start a conversation with a stranger, and sometimes people do not notice that another person needs to get past them. But I do not think this makes them unfriendly. On a crowded train, most people would not talk to each other anyway. Headphones simply give them a little private space in a noisy place, and that can make them calmer and more patient. The important thing is to stay aware, for example by keeping the volume low and taking the headphones off when someone speaks to you.

listening.script: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people say that wearing headphones in public places makes people less friendly and less aware of others. Do you agree or disagree? Why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I think schools should give every student the chance to learn an instrument, but I would not make it a requirement for many years. Learning an instrument teaches patience, because you improve only through regular practice, and playing in a group teaches students to listen to each other. For those reasons, one or two years of lessons in primary school would be valuable for everyone. After that, students should be free to choose. If teenagers are forced to continue with an instrument they dislike, the lessons become a punishment, and that time could be spent on art, sports, or another skill.

listening.script: Here is my last question. Do you think every school should require students to learn a musical instrument? Why or why not?
